scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: Lightning hits tall buildings all the time, yet most of them don't catch fire or crack. What protects them?

scenes.name: charge
scenes.text: Inside storm clouds, ice and water collide, and separate electric charge. The bottom of the cloud usually becomes negative.

scenes.name: strike
scenes.text: When the charge gets big enough, it jumps to the ground as lightning. A typical bolt carries around thirty thousand amps.

scenes.name: rod
scenes.text: A lightning conductor is a metal rod on the highest point of the building, connected to a thick metal strip running down the side.

scenes.name: ground
scenes.text: That strip ends in metal rods or plates buried deep in the earth. So the current takes this easy path, instead of through the walls.

scenes.name: myth
scenes.text: It doesn't attract lightning from far away. It just gives a strike nearby a safe route to the ground.

scenes.name: you
scenes.text: Outdoors in a storm, avoid tall trees and open fields, and get inside a building or a car with a metal roof.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Charge, strike, rod, ground. A safe road for lightning. Follow for more on how things really work.
